segments.title: The scenario and the basics
sections: The Basics You Skip On A Busy Morning

cues.text: It is Tuesday. You have read every page on levels, reads and triggers, and you sit down at 9:27 a.m. with no idea written.
You take a trade from a price you noticed. You nudge the stop when price gets close. You never grade it.
None of that was a gap in knowledge. Each one was a basic you knew and skipped, on the morning it mattered.
You did not forget what a trigger is. You skipped it, with great confidence.
Now, the habit. You brush your teeth without deciding to. It happens at the same point every day, and missing it feels wrong.
This module sets out eight trading habits to run the same way. Not strategies. Not secrets. Routines, done every session.
Each one is a line on your sheet, the one page you fill in before the open, or a field in your journal. So you can see whether you ran it, instead of trusting that you did.
The eight fall into four parts of the day, mechanical first.
Before the open: four habits.
At the entry: two.
After the exit: one.
And last, around your desk: the people. That one is about you, not the chart.
The rule: a habit counts only when it leaves a line on paper every session, whatever the day did.
Getting it wrong is a habit you believe in and cannot show. It reveals you are trusting memory, and memory agrees with how the day ended.
The fix: no line on paper, no habit. Count only what you can point to.

segments.title: Before the open: idea, two plans, one goal
sections: Before The Open: Your Idea, Two Plans And One Goal

cues.text: Four habits, all on the sheet before 9:25 a.m.
One: know your idea. If price reaches a named level, you do this, and you are wrong at this price.
Name the level by its slug, the short name you log it under, like pd-high. The invalidation is the price that ends the idea.
Add a conviction, counted not felt: one point for each of three checks.
No day-type call. Trend day is a label no price at 9:45 can prove wrong.
The rule: the idea is on paper before 9:25 a.m., with a slug, an invalidation and a counted conviction.
Getting it wrong is writing feels like a trend day up. A forecast came first, and every bar will be read to agree.
The fix: write the idea backwards, invalidation first.
Two: have a plan. One or more branches and a nothing case. It says what you do at each place price can go, never where it will go.
A branch reads: if price does this at a slug, and the trigger fires, you do that. You are wrong at this price.
Getting it wrong is looking for longs. That is not a plan. It is a mood.
The fix: every branch begins with if, names a slug, and carries an invalidation price. Cross out any line missing one.
Three: have a second plan. Price can reach the other side, so write a branch there too.
Between the branches sits the nothing case: a price range with two numbers, ending in no trade.
The rule: a branch on each side of price, and a nothing case.
Getting it wrong is one branch, long, and nothing below price. The side you did not write gets filled by impulse.
Four: set your process goal, from one weakness in your last weekly review.
One sentence about what you do, never what you make. Say it aloud: Today you enter only after the trigger fires at a level on the plan.
The rule: one goal, marked kept or not kept at the close.
Getting it wrong is make two R today. That is a wish about the result, so nothing you do can be checked.
The fix: name an action the journal records, like the trigger field or the stop price.

segments.title: At the entry, and after the exit
sections: At The Entry: Your Setups And Your Stop
After The Exit: Review And Grade Every Trade

cues.text: Five: only trade your setups. A setup is yours when it sits on your plan as a branch and in your journal as a slug.
The rule: every entry matches a branch you wrote before 9:25 a.m.
Getting it wrong is a midday trade from a price you found on the screen, or one copied from a chat. It reveals the screen became the plan the moment the plan went quiet.
The fix: before the order is armed, read the branch it comes from aloud. No branch to read, no order. A trade taken anyway is tagged No Setup, the journal tag for a trade taken on feel.
Six: honour your stop.
The stop is a resting order behind the zone's far edge, sent with the entry as a bracket: an entry and its stop, sent together.
It is never widened or pulled to breakeven by hand. The one planned scale is the only change the plan allows.
The rule: every trade has its stop resting from the moment of entry, at the price the plan wrote, until the trade ends.
A stop you can move is not a stop. It is a suggestion.

Getting it wrong is a stop dragged two points further away as price closes in, or tightened to breakeven to be safe. It reveals the stop is being treated as an opinion, so the risk you sized for is not the risk you carry.

The fix: the order template sends the stop with the entry, with automatic breakeven off. A widened stop is tagged Broke Rule, the tag for a broken hard rule. A stop moved closer and hit is tagged Too Early, a manual exit for none of the four reasons on the Pass list.
Seven: review and grade every trade.
The grade is A plus, A, B or C, given at entry from four checks, before the trade resolves.
Then, after the exit, the execution mark: Pass or Fail.
The rule: every trade is graded at entry and marked the same day, with one line in your own words.
Getting it wrong is grading only the losers, or a week of trades marked on Sunday from memory. It reveals the review is chasing pain instead of recording decisions.
The fix: the grade is filled before the exit, and the end-of-day routine is not finished while any trade of the day has an empty mark.

segments.title: Around the desk, and the worked case
sections: Around The Desk: Find Your People
Worked Case: One Session, Eight Lines

cues.text: Eight: find your people. Find a trading partner or group that speaks the language, after the session. The sheet is yours. Before 9:25 a.m., nothing from anyone else goes on it.
What you share is your record, not your calls. Once a week: the review's counts, your grades, your marks, your Too Early count and your Broke Rule ledger. And you read theirs.
This is the hard one, because the pull toward other traders is strongest on the mornings your own sheet looks uncertain.
The chat is very sure of itself. That is not the same as being right.
The rule: outside views stay closed until after the close, and once a week you exchange review fields with a partner or group.

Getting it wrong is opening the chat at 8:50 and adding a branch at 9:24 that matches a post. It reveals you are asking someone else to carry the uncertainty, so the idea on the sheet is no longer yours to grade.
The fix: chats, feeds and notes stay closed until the close. The weekly exchange uses the review sheet's lines and nothing else: no screenshots of P and L, and no calls for your next session.
Now, the worked case. A composite MNQ session, built to show each habit as a line on paper. It belongs to no one, and the prices are invented.
One: the idea, on the sheet by 9:21 a.m., with its slug, its invalidation and its counted conviction.
Two and three: an idea on each side of price, and a nothing case between them with two numbers, ending in no trade.
Four: the process goal, said aloud at 9:15, taken from the last weekly review.
Five: the entry matches the first idea. A fast move off an unmarked price gets one line in the notes and no order.
Six: the stop goes with the entry as a bracket, and it is not touched. Seven: the grade at entry and the mark after the exit, both written the same day.
Eight: no chat opened before the close. On Sunday, the week's review lines go to a partner.
Eight lines, all on paper. Where price went after the exit is not on any of them.

cues.text: Take your last five sessions. Score one point for each habit that left its line on paper in all five.
One: know your idea, written before 9:25 a.m.
Two: a plan, with a branch in the if form.
Three: a second plan, and a nothing case with two numbers.
Four: a process goal, marked kept or not kept.
Five: every entry matched a branch, with no No Setup tags.
Six: every stop rested from entry to exit at its planned price.
Seven: every trade graded at entry and marked the same day.
Eight: no outside view before the close, and review fields exchanged that week.
Eight of eight: the habits are running. Keep them running.
Six or seven: the missing habit is next week's process goal.
Under six: start with lines one and seven. One sets what you will do. Seven records whether you did it.
One override: a miss on line six makes the stop next week's process goal, whatever the total.
Nobody has ever lost sleep over a sheet that was filled in on time.
Now, before your next session.
Before 9:25 a.m., write one process goal at the top of your sheet. One sentence that starts: Today you. Say it aloud once. That is the whole assignment.
Where it goes next.
Each habit has a home. The idea and its counted conviction come from Module 9. The two plans and the nothing case come from Module 15, written each morning on the sheet in Module 16.
The stop is built in Module 14. The grade, the mark and the weekly review that picks your process goal are in Module 18.
Module 20 picks up the habits under pressure: the post-loss reset, the loops a bad day runs, and the readiness score.
